# My Thinking

My family has farmed this land in Quzhou for as long as I can remember. Every household around me grows winter wheat and summer maize on the same fields, one after the other. That is what I know, and that is what works here on the North China Plain.

My land is about 8 mu. I will plant all of it to winter wheat this autumn, then after I harvest the wheat in June, I will put summer maize on the same fields right away. This double-cropping is what everyone does. The government has a price support for wheat, so there is less risk. Maize feeds the animals and brings cash.

For wheat, I will use the Jimai variety seeds I buy from the county seed station — improved but not hybrid, because wheat doesn't work that way. I'll rotary-till after the maize is harvested in September to break up the stubble before I sow. I apply compound fertilizer as a base before planting, then I top-dress with urea at jointing. My neighbor uses about 18 jin of nitrogen per mu and his yields are good, so I do the same. I will irrigate four times: once before sowing to wet the soil, once in winter to protect the roots from freezing, once at jointing, and once at heading. I'll spray herbicide once and fungicide once for powdery mildew — two applications total.

For maize, I always buy Zhengdan 958 or Xianyu 335 hybrid seed from the town. After wheat harvest, I don't have time to plow, so I direct-seed into the stubble — no-till. I apply urea in two splits. Summer rains usually water the maize, but I'll pump once from the tube well if July is dry. I spray herbicide right after emergence and then check for corn borers later in the season.

My expected yields are around 450 kg/mu for wheat and 550 kg/mu for maize — about what I got last year.
